lines.text: Your ad has three seconds before someone scrolls past it forever. Here's the exact formula for making those three seconds count.

Seconds one to three — the pattern interrupt. You need to say or show something that makes their thumb stop. Not your logo. Not your company name. Something that speaks directly to a problem they're already living. A plumber who opens with 'water bill gone up lately?' stops more scrolls than 'ABC Plumbing, serving your area.' Start with them. Not you.

Seconds four to twenty — one clear piece of value. Not three tips. Not a full service rundown. One insight that makes them think: I didn't know that, or — that's exactly my problem. The moment someone learns something from your ad, you become the authority. That's when trust begins and they keep watching.

Last ten seconds — one clear next step. Not 'visit the website' and 'give us a call' and 'follow for more tips.' One action. The more options you give them, the less likely they are to do any of them. Pick the one you want and make it as easy as possible to take.

lines.text: Most service businesses are losing leads because their lead form asks for too much, too soon. I'm gonna show you exactly how to set this up so people actually fill it out.

First thing — keep the required fields to three, maximum. Phone, name, and the service they need. That's it. Everything else is friction. You can ask for address or details after they submit. Most people won't complete a form that feels like a mortgage application.

Second — use the pre-fill feature. Meta knows their phone number. Let it auto-populate. Same with name if they're logged in. You're cutting down typing. Less typing means higher submission rate. This alone usually lifts conversions by 15 to 20 percent.

Third — your confirmation message matters. Tell them exactly what to expect. 'A technician will call you within two hours' or 'You'll get a text in the next 10 minutes.' People want to know what happens next. A vague thank you costs you follow-ups.
The difference between a 20 percent submission rate and a 50 percent submission rate is usually just three things: fewer fields, pre-fill enabled, and clear expectations. That's it.

lines.text: everyone asks me this — should I run Meta or Google? and the answer is never just one or the other.

Google is intent-based. Someone types in 'plumber near me' or 'HVAC repair' — boom, they're actively looking. That's high intent. But you're competing with everyone else who shows up in that search, so it can get expensive.

Meta is discovery-based. Someone's scrolling their feed, not thinking about your service yet, and your ad pops up at exactly the right moment. The cost per lead is usually lower because you're finding people before they're desperate.

For most service businesses — plumbers, electricians, window cleaners, detailers — Meta typically wins on budget efficiency. But if you want someone ready to book *right now*, Google gets you there. Real answer? Run both, but start with what your budget can handle.
Most of my clients do better with Meta first because the math is cleaner. But your business might be different — depends on your market, your service, and how fast you want to scale.

The best headline is just the truth about what your customer wants, written the way they'd actually say it.
